learner:
Beginner-intermediate guitarist who plays by ear and knows open chords and a few barre chords.
Goal: understand keys and chords well enough to write original chord progressions.
Cannot read notation, so lessons use frets, letter names and numbers instead of staff notation.
Can name the notes of C major. Guessed correctly that a key has seven chords but doesn't know why.
Gaps: doesn't know what makes a chord minor, and hasn't learned intervals, triad construction, or Roman numerals.

lessons.title: Half Steps and Whole Steps on the Fretboard
lessons.objective: Count half and whole steps on a string and name the notes between letter names.
lessons.hook: Every scale and chord is built from these two distances, and your fretboard already shows them.
lessons.explain: Music measures distance in half steps. A half step is the distance of one fret on the same string. A whole step is two half steps, or two frets. Play the open A string, then fret 2: A to B is a whole step. Fret 3 gives C, only a half step above B. E to F and B to C are half steps; every other pair of neighboring letter names is a whole step. The gaps get sharps or flats. A sharp (#) raises a note one half step; a flat (b) lowers it one half step, so A string fret 1 is A# or Bb. There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats an octave higher, which is why fret 12 is A again.
key_facts: A half step is the distance of one fret on the same string.
A whole step is two half steps, or two frets.
There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats an octave higher.
E to F and B to C are half steps; every other pair of neighboring letter names is a whole step.
A sharp (#) raises a note one half step; a flat (b) lowers it one half step.

predict.q: On the A string, which fret gives the note C?

angles: Think of the piano: white keys with a black key between them are a whole step apart, and E–F and B–C have no black key between them, so they are a half step apart.
Walk up the low E string one fret at a time: E, F, F#, G, G#, A, A#, B, C, C#, D, D#, E. That is 12 steps back to E, and there is nothing between E and F or between B and C.
claims: One fret on guitar equals one half step.
A whole step equals two half steps.
There are 12 distinct notes in Western tuning before the octave.
E–F and B–C are half steps.
A sharp raises a note a half step and a flat lowers it a half step.

items.q: You move from fret 5 to fret 6 on the same string. How far did you move?
items.why: One fret on the same string is one half step.
misconceptions: Thinks one fret is a whole step
Confuses a single fret with a larger interval
Thinks each fret counts as two half steps

items.q: Which move is a whole step?
items.why: A whole step is two frets.
misconceptions: Thinks one fret is a whole step
Thinks a whole step spans four frets
Doesn't see that a distance requires movement

items.q: Which pair of neighboring notes is only a half step apart?
items.why: E–F and B–C are the only neighboring letters a half step apart.
misconceptions: Thinks every pair of neighboring letters is a half step
Believes F–G has no note between them
Believes A–B has no note between them

items.q: Which name refers to the same note as Db?
items.why: A flat lowers D one half step, which lands on the note a sharp raises C to.
misconceptions: Thinks a flat raises a note
Thinks a flat lowers a note by a whole step
Confuses which letter the flat belongs to

items.q: How many different notes are there before the pattern repeats an octave higher?
items.why: Twelve half steps bring you back to the same letter an octave up.

items.q: Name both pairs of neighboring letter-name notes that are a half step apart.
accept: E to F and B to C
items.why: All other neighboring letter pairs are a whole step apart.

lessons.title: The Major Scale Formula
lessons.objective: Build a major scale on any starting note using the step pattern.
lessons.hook: Know one pattern and you can find the notes of any key, not just C.
lessons.explain: The major scale follows the step pattern W W H W W W H (whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half). Starting the pattern on any note gives that note's major scale. From C you get C D E F G A B, so C major uses only natural notes: C D E F G A B, because its half steps land exactly on E–F and B–C. Try G: G A B C D E. A whole step above E is F#, then a half step reaches G. So G major needs one sharp, F#, to keep the pattern. Each letter name appears exactly once in a major scale, which is why that note is written F# and not Gb.
key_facts: The major scale follows the step pattern W W H W W W H.
Starting the pattern on any note gives that note's major scale.
C major uses only natural notes: C D E F G A B.
G major needs one sharp, F#, to keep the pattern.
Each letter name appears exactly once in a major scale.

predict.q: Building G major with W W H W W W H, what note comes right after E?

angles: Play the pattern up a single string: from the open string go up 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 frets. On the low E string that gives E F# G# A B C# D# E, which is E major.
The pattern is two groups split by half steps: W W H, then W W W H. The half steps always fall between degrees 3–4 and 7–8.

rungs.text: Build D major. D +W = E, +W = F#, +H = G, +W = A, +W = B, +W = C#, +H = D. Result: D E F# G A B C#.
Build A major. A +W = B, +W = ___, +H = D, +W = E, +W = ___, +W = ___, +H = A.
Build F major with W W H W W W H, using each letter name once.

claims: The major scale step pattern is W W H W W W H.
C major contains no sharps or flats.
G major has one sharp, F#.
D major is D E F# G A B C#.
A major scale uses each letter name once.

items.q: Which is the major scale step pattern?
options: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
W W W H W W H
H W W W H W W
items.answer: W W H W W W H
items.why: That is the fixed pattern for every major scale.
misconceptions: Confuses the major pattern with the natural minor pattern
Puts the first half step in the wrong place
Thinks the scale starts with a half step

items.q: Which is the D major scale?
options: D E F# G A B C#
D E F G A B C
D E F# G A Bb C
D E F# G# A B C#
items.answer: D E F# G A B C#
items.why: Applying W W H W W W H from D gives F# and C#.
misconceptions: Thinks every scale uses only natural notes like C major
Applies the pattern correctly at first, then loses track
Puts a whole step where the half step belongs between degrees 3 and 4

items.q: Why does G major contain F# rather than F?
options: The pattern needs a whole step from E
G major always borrows notes from D
F is too close to the starting note
Sharps make a scale sound happier
items.answer: The pattern needs a whole step from E
items.why: Degrees 6 to 7 must be a whole step, and E to F is only a half step.
misconceptions: Thinks the sharp comes from another key
Thinks notes are chosen by how close they are
Thinks sharps are added for mood rather than structure

items.q: In A major, why is the note between F# and A written G# and not Ab?
options: Each letter must appear exactly once
Flats are never used in major scales
G# is higher in pitch than Ab
Ab belongs only to minor scales
items.answer: Each letter must appear exactly once
items.why: Writing Ab would repeat the letter A and skip G.
misconceptions: Thinks major scales cannot contain flats
Thinks G# and Ab are different pitches
Thinks spelling depends on whether the key is major or minor

items.q: List the notes of C major.
items.answer: C D E F G A B
accept: C, D, E, F, G, A, B
items.why: C major uses only natural notes.

items.q: What is the one sharp in G major?
items.why: F# keeps the whole step between degrees 6 and 7.

lessons.title: Scale Degrees
lessons.objective: Number the notes of any major scale and name degrees 1, 4 and 5.
lessons.hook: Numbers let you think about every key at once instead of memorizing letters.
lessons.explain: Scale degrees number the notes of a scale 1 through 7 from the starting note. In C major, C is 1, D is 2, and so on up to B as 7. Degree 1 is called the tonic, the home note of the key. Degree 4 is called the subdominant. Degree 5 is called the dominant. Numbers let one pattern work in every key: degree 5 is G in C major and D in G major. When musicians say 'go to the five,' they mean the same relationship in every key.
key_facts: Scale degrees number the notes of a scale 1 through 7 from the starting note.
Degree 1 is called the tonic, the home note of the key.
Degree 5 is called the dominant.
Degree 4 is called the subdominant.
Numbers let one pattern work in every key: degree 5 is G in C major and D in G major.
angles: Scale degrees are like seat numbers. The letters change from key to key, but seat 1 is always the home note.
In G major (G A B C D E F#), counting up from G gives C as 4 and D as 5.
claims: Degree 1 is the tonic.
Degree 4 is the subdominant.
Degree 5 is the dominant.
Degree 5 in C major is G.
Degree 5 in G major is D.

items.q: In D major (D E F# G A B C#), which note is degree 3?
items.why: Counting from D as 1, the third note is F#.
misconceptions: Started counting from 0
Counted the fourth note
Counted the fifth note

items.q: What is degree 1 of a key called?
items.why: The tonic is the home note.
misconceptions: Confuses degree 1 with degree 5
Confuses degree 1 with degree 4
Invents a term for degree 1

items.q: In G major, which note is the dominant?
items.why: The dominant is degree 5, and degree 5 of G major is D.
misconceptions: Confuses the dominant with the subdominant
Thinks the dominant is the tonic
Counts the second note

items.q: Which degree is the subdominant?
items.why: Degree 4 is named the subdominant.
misconceptions: Confuses the subdominant with the dominant
Thinks 'sub' means the step just above the tonic
Guesses at random

items.q: What is degree 5 called, and which note is it in C major?
items.why: Counting C D E F G, the fifth note is G.

items.q: Why do musicians use scale-degree numbers instead of letter names?
items.answer: Numbers let one pattern work in every key, so 'degree 5' means the same relationship whatever the key.
accept: They describe the same relationship in any key
So a pattern can be moved to any key
items.why: Letters change from key to key, but degree relationships stay the same.

lessons.title: Intervals: Thirds and Fifths
lessons.objective: Measure major thirds, minor thirds, perfect fifths and diminished fifths in half steps.
lessons.hook: Chords are built from these four distances, so knowing them explains every chord you play.
lessons.explain: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. A major third is 4 half steps, like C to E. A minor third is 3 half steps, like C to Eb. A perfect fifth is 7 half steps, like C to G. A diminished fifth is 6 half steps, like B to F. On one string, count frets: from fret 3, a major third is fret 7 and a perfect fifth is fret 10.
key_facts: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps.
A major third is 4 half steps, like C to E.
A minor third is 3 half steps, like C to Eb.
A perfect fifth is 7 half steps, like C to G.
A diminished fifth is 6 half steps, like B to F.
angles: Power chords are a root plus a perfect fifth: the root on one string and the fifth two frets up on the next string, which is 7 half steps.
A major third and a minor third differ by exactly one fret, or 4 half steps versus 3.
claims: A major third is 4 half steps.
A minor third is 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth is 7 half steps.
A diminished fifth is 6 half steps.
B to F is a diminished fifth.

items.q: How many half steps are in a minor third?
items.why: A minor third is 3 half steps.
misconceptions: Confuses the minor third with the major third
Confuses a third with a whole step
Confuses a third with a fourth

items.q: Which pair of notes is a major third apart?
items.why: C to E is 4 half steps.
misconceptions: Confuses the major third with the minor third
Confuses a third with a fifth
Confuses a third with a whole step

items.q: From fret 5, which fret is a perfect fifth higher on the same string?
items.why: A perfect fifth is 7 half steps, and 5 + 7 = 12.
misconceptions: Counts a fifth as 5 half steps
Treats the perfect fifth as 6 half steps
Counts a major third

items.q: What is the interval from B to F?
items.why: B to F is 6 half steps.
misconceptions: Assumes every five-letter span is a perfect fifth
Confuses fifths with thirds
Confuses fifths with thirds

items.q: What unit do we use to count interval sizes?
items.why: An interval is the distance between notes, measured in half steps.

items.q: How many half steps are in a perfect fifth, and what is the perfect fifth above C?
items.why: C to G spans 7 half steps.

lessons.title: What Makes a Chord Major or Minor
lessons.objective: Build major and minor triads from intervals and explain the difference between them.
lessons.hook: Changing a single note turns a happy chord into a sad one, and knowing which note gives you control.
lessons.explain: A triad is three notes: a root, a third, and a fifth. A major triad is a root, a major third (4 half steps), and a perfect fifth (7 half steps). A minor triad is a root, a minor third (3 half steps), and a perfect fifth. The only difference between a major and a minor triad is the third, lowered one half step. Try it: E major is E G# B; E minor is E G B. In the open E chord, your first finger on the G string (fret 1) plays G#. Lift that finger to play the open G string, and the chord becomes Em.
key_facts: A triad is three notes: a root, a third, and a fifth.
A major triad is a root, a major third (4 half steps), and a perfect fifth (7 half steps).
A minor triad is a root, a minor third (3 half steps), and a perfect fifth.
The only difference between a major and a minor triad is the third, lowered one half step.
E major is E G# B; E minor is E G B.
fixes: Did not know what makes a chord minor. A minor chord has a minor third (3 half steps) above the root instead of a major third (4 half steps), while the root and fifth stay the same.

predict.q: You play an open E chord and lift the finger on the G string. What happens?

angles: Compare open A and open Am. The only finger that moves is on the B string, which goes from C# (fret 2) to C (fret 1). That move is the third dropping a half step.
Major is built 4 + 3 half steps, and minor is built 3 + 4. Both add up to 7, the perfect fifth.
claims: A major triad has a major third and a perfect fifth.
A minor triad has a minor third and a perfect fifth.
E major is E G# B.
E minor is E G B.
In an open E chord, fret 1 on the G string is G#.

items.q: What makes a triad minor?
options: Its third is 3 half steps above the root
Its fifth is lowered a half step
Its root is a flat note
It is played lower on the neck
items.answer: Its third is 3 half steps above the root
items.why: A minor triad has a minor third and a perfect fifth.
misconceptions: Confuses minor with diminished
Thinks the root's name decides the quality
Thinks quality depends on where it is played

items.q: Which note changes when C major (C E G) becomes C minor?
items.why: Only the third is lowered, by one half step.
misconceptions: Thinks the fifth is what changes
Thinks the root is what changes
Thinks the third is raised

items.q: Which set of notes is a major triad?
items.why: A to C# is 4 half steps and A to E is 7.
misconceptions: Mistakes the minor third for a major third
Doesn't check the fifth
Thinks any three notes make a triad

items.q: Which spelling is E minor?
items.why: E to G is a minor third and E to B is a perfect fifth.
misconceptions: Confuses E minor with E major
Confuses minor with diminished
Uses a fourth instead of a third

items.q: Name the three notes of a triad by their role.
items.why: A triad stacks a third and a fifth above a root.

items.q: Explain what makes a chord minor rather than major.
items.answer: Its third is a minor third (3 half steps above the root) instead of a major third (4 half steps). The root and the fifth are the same.
accept: The third is lowered one half step
A minor third above the root with a perfect fifth
items.why: The third is the only note that differs.

lessons.title: The Diminished Triad
lessons.objective: Recognize and spell a diminished triad.
lessons.hook: Every major key contains one diminished chord, so you'll need to know it.
lessons.explain: A diminished triad is a root, a minor third, and a diminished fifth (6 half steps). In other words, a diminished triad is two minor thirds stacked. B diminished is B D F: B to D is 3 half steps, and D to F is 3 more. Diminished is written with a small circle, as in B°. Its tense sound makes it want to move to another chord, so it's usually passed through rather than rested on.
key_facts: A diminished triad is a root, a minor third, and a diminished fifth (6 half steps).
B diminished is B D F.
Diminished is written with a small circle, as in B°.
A diminished triad is two minor thirds stacked.
Its tense sound makes it want to move to another chord.
angles: Start from a minor triad and lower its fifth one half step. Bm is B D F#, so B° is B D F.
Major is 4+3, minor is 3+4, and diminished is 3+3.
claims: A diminished triad has a minor third and a diminished fifth.
B diminished is B D F.
The ° symbol means diminished.

items.q: Which spelling is B diminished?
items.why: B to D is a minor third and B to F is a diminished fifth.
misconceptions: Confuses diminished with minor
Confuses diminished with major
Doesn't stack thirds

items.q: How large is the fifth in a diminished triad?
items.why: A diminished fifth is 6 half steps.
misconceptions: Thinks it has a perfect fifth
Confuses it with a fourth
Confuses it with an augmented fifth

items.q: What does the symbol in C° mean?
items.why: The small circle marks a diminished chord.
misconceptions: Confuses ° with the major seventh triangle
Thinks ° means minor
Thinks ° means a two-note chord

items.q: Which interval stack builds a diminished triad?
items.why: A diminished triad is two stacked minor thirds.
misconceptions: Describes a major triad
Describes a minor triad
Describes an augmented triad

items.q: List the three intervals-from-the-root that define a diminished triad.
items.why: That combination is the definition of diminished.

items.q: How does a diminished chord usually behave in a progression?
items.answer: It sounds tense and wants to move to another chord.
accept: It is unstable and resolves to another chord
items.why: The diminished fifth creates tension.

lessons.title: Building Chords from a Scale
lessons.objective: Stack every other scale note to build and name the triad on any degree of a major key.
lessons.hook: This shows exactly which chords belong in a key, so you can stop guessing.
lessons.explain: To build a chord in a key, start on a scale note and stack every other scale note: 1-3-5. Using only scale notes, the C major scale gives C E G, D F A, E G B, F A C, G B D, A C E, B D F. One triad starts on each of the seven scale degrees, so a major key has seven basic chords. Measuring the third and fifth of each stack tells you its quality. For example, D F A is minor because D to F is 3 half steps, and D to A is a perfect fifth.
key_facts: To build a chord in a key, start on a scale note and stack every other scale note: 1-3-5.
Using only scale notes, the C major scale gives C E G, D F A, E G B, F A C, G B D, A C E, B D F.
One triad starts on each of the seven scale degrees, so a major key has seven basic chords.
Measuring the third and fifth of each stack tells you its quality.
D F A is minor because D to F is 3 half steps.
fixes: Guessed that a key has seven chords without knowing why. One triad is built on each of the seven scale degrees.

predict.q: Stacking every other note of C major starting on E, which chord do you get?

angles: Write the scale twice in a row (C D E F G A B C D E F G A B). Then, from any starting note, take one note, skip one, take one, skip one, take one.
Every chord comes from the same seven notes, which is why they all sound like they belong together.

rungs.text: Chord on degree 2 of G major (G A B C D E F#): start on A, skip B, take C, skip D, take E, giving A C E. A to C is 3 half steps and A to E is 7, so it's A minor.
Chord on degree 5 of G major: start on ___, then take ___ and ___. D to F# is ___ half steps, so the chord is ___.
Build and name the chord on degree 7 of G major.

claims: Diatonic triads are built by stacking scale notes a third apart.
The triad on degree 2 of C major is D F A.
D F A is a minor triad.
A major key has seven diatonic triads.
The triad on degree 7 of G major is F# A C.

items.q: In C major, which notes form the chord built on G?
items.why: Take every other scale note from G: G, B, D.
misconceptions: Stacks neighboring notes instead of skipping
Uses a note that is not in the key
Builds a different chord shape

items.q: In C major, which triad starts on A?
items.why: Stacking every other C-major note from A gives A C E.
misconceptions: Assumes every chord is major and uses a note outside the key
Stacks neighboring notes
Uses a fourth instead of a third

items.q: Why does a major key have seven basic chords?
options: One triad is built on each scale degree
Seven chord shapes fit on the guitar
It is a convention with no reason
items.answer: One triad is built on each scale degree
items.why: Seven scale degrees give seven starting notes.
misconceptions: Thinks the guitar decides theory
Confuses chord size with the number of chords
Thinks the count is arbitrary

items.q: Why is the C-major chord D F A minor?
options: D to F is 3 half steps
D to A is 6 half steps
items.answer: D to F is 3 half steps
items.why: A minor third over a perfect fifth makes a minor triad.
misconceptions: Gets the fifth wrong
Thinks F is a flat
Gives the position as the cause instead of the intervals

items.q: How do you build a triad on a scale degree using only notes from the key?
items.answer: Start on that scale note and stack every other scale note (1-3-5).
accept: Take a note, skip one, take one, skip one, take one
items.why: Stacking thirds within the scale keeps every note in the key.

items.q: How do you work out whether a stacked triad is major, minor or diminished?
items.answer: Measure the third and fifth above the root in half steps.
accept: Check the intervals from the root
items.why: The intervals define the quality.

lessons.title: The Seven Chords of a Major Key
lessons.objective: List the seven chords of any major key using the quality pattern.
lessons.hook: Memorize one pattern and you know the chords of every major key instantly.
lessons.explain: In every major key the chord qualities run major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. In C major the seven chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, and B°. Chords on degrees 1, 4, and 5 are major. Chords on degrees 2, 3, and 6 are minor. The chord on degree 7 is diminished. Apply the pattern to G major's scale and you get G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F#°, the same pattern on new letters.
key_facts: In every major key the chord qualities run major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
In C major the seven chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, and B°.
Chords on degrees 1, 4, and 5 are major.
Chords on degrees 2, 3, and 6 are minor.
The chord on degree 7 is diminished.
In G major the chords are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, and F#°.
fixes: Guessed that a key has seven chords without knowing why. One triad is built on each of the seven scale degrees.

predict.q: Which chord is NOT in the key of G major?

angles: G–C–D–Em are the common campfire chords, and they are degrees 1, 4, 5 and 6 of G major.
The pattern never changes because the step pattern of the major scale never changes.
claims: Major keys follow the pattern maj, min, min, maj, maj, min, dim.
C major's chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°.
G major's chords are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F#°.

items.q: Which is the chord-quality pattern of a major key?
options: maj min min maj maj min dim
maj min maj min maj min dim
min maj maj min min maj dim
maj maj min maj min min dim
items.answer: maj min min maj maj min dim
items.why: This is the fixed pattern for degrees 1 to 7.
misconceptions: Thinks the qualities simply alternate
Reverses major and minor
Remembers the pattern only loosely

items.q: Which chord belongs to C major?
items.why: Degree 2 in C is D minor.
misconceptions: Thinks every chord in a key is major
Doesn't know degree 3 is minor
Doesn't know degree 4 is major

items.q: Which degrees carry major chords?
items.why: Degrees 1, 4 and 5 are major in every major key.
misconceptions: Confuses these with the notes of the tonic triad
Picks the even-numbered degrees
Thinks degree 6 is major

items.q: Which set lists the minor chords in G major?
items.why: Degrees 2, 3 and 6 of G are A, B and E.
misconceptions: Makes degrees 4 and 5 minor
Thinks degree 5 is minor
Thinks the tonic chord is minor

items.q: What quality is the chord on degree 7 of a major key?
items.why: Degree 7 forms two stacked minor thirds.

items.q: How many basic chords does a major key have, and why?
items.answer: Seven, because one triad is built on each of the seven scale degrees.
items.why: Each degree is the root of one chord.

lessons.title: Roman Numeral Chord Names
lessons.objective: Write and read progressions in Roman numerals and move them to any key.
lessons.hook: Roman numerals let you write a progression once and play it in any key.
lessons.explain: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree: I through VII. Uppercase numerals mean major chords and lowercase mean minor chords. A small circle after a lowercase numeral means diminished, as in vii°. So the major-key chords are written I ii iii IV V vi vii°. A numeral progression like I–V–vi–IV can be played in any key: in C it is C–G–Am–F, in G it is G–D–Em–C.
key_facts: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree: I through VII.
Uppercase numerals mean major chords and lowercase mean minor chords.
A small circle after a lowercase numeral means diminished, as in vii°.
The major-key chords are written I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
A numeral progression like I–V–vi–IV can be played in any key: in C it is C–G–Am–F, in G it is G–D–Em–C.
angles: Think of it like a capo. Using a capo moves the same shapes to a new key, and Roman numerals move the same progression to a new key.
Big numerals mean big, bright major chords, and small numerals mean minor chords.
claims: Uppercase Roman numerals mean major chords.
Lowercase Roman numerals mean minor chords.
I–V–vi–IV in C is C–G–Am–F.
I–V–vi–IV in G is G–D–Em–C.

items.q: What does a lowercase 'ii' tell you?
items.why: Lowercase numerals mean minor chords.
misconceptions: Ignores the letter case
Confuses minor with diminished
Confuses numerals with inversions

items.q: Which line correctly writes the major-key chords?
options: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
I II III IV V VI VII
i ii iii iv v vi vii
I ii III IV v vi VII°
items.answer: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
items.why: Case and the circle show the maj-min-min-maj-maj-min-dim pattern.
misconceptions: Thinks every chord is major
Thinks every chord is minor
Mixes up which degrees are major

items.q: What is I–V–vi–IV in G major?
items.why: In G, degrees 1, 5, 6 and 4 are G, D, Em and C.
misconceptions: Ignores the lowercase vi
Swaps IV and V
Miscounts degree 6

items.q: What do Roman numerals represent in chord names?
items.answer: The scale degree each chord is built on.
accept: the chord's root as a scale degree
items.why: I through VII match degrees 1 through 7.

items.q: Write I–V–vi–IV in C major.
items.why: Degrees 1, 5, 6 and 4 of C are C, G, A minor and F.

lessons.title: Chord Functions: Home, Away, Tension
lessons.objective: Use tonic, subdominant and dominant functions to plan a progression that sounds resolved.
lessons.hook: Functions explain why some progressions feel finished and others leave you hanging.
lessons.explain: The I chord is the tonic: it sounds like home and resolution. The IV chord is the subdominant: it moves away from home, often leading to V. The V chord is the dominant: it creates tension that pulls back to I. So I–IV–V–I is the basic home–away–tension–home progression. In G, that's G–C–D–G. Try stopping on the D and notice how unfinished it sounds. vi can stand in for I because they share two notes: Am (A C E) and C (C E G) share C and E.
key_facts: The I chord is the tonic: it sounds like home and resolution.
The V chord is the dominant: it creates tension that pulls back to I.
The IV chord is the subdominant: it moves away from home, often leading to V.
I–IV–V–I is the basic home–away–tension–home progression.
vi can stand in for I because they share two notes; Am (A C E) and C (C E G) share C and E.

predict.q: In C major, which chord makes a progression feel finished when you end on it?

angles: A progression works like a short trip. I is your house, IV is a walk out, V is the turn back toward home, and I is arriving home.
Play E–A–B and stop. The B chord (V in E) leaves you hanging until you play E.
claims: I is the tonic chord.
IV is the subdominant chord.
V is the dominant chord and tends to resolve to I.
Am and C share the notes C and E.

items.q: Which chord creates the strongest pull back to I?
items.why: The dominant creates tension that resolves to I.
misconceptions: Confuses the subdominant with the dominant
Overrates the pull of ii
Confuses the substitute for home with tension

items.q: In D major, which chord is the subdominant?

misconceptions: Confuses the subdominant with the dominant
Picks degree 2
Picks degree 6

items.q: Why can Am replace C in the key of C?
options: They share the notes C and E
Am is the dominant of C
items.answer: They share the notes C and E
items.why: Two of their three notes are the same.
misconceptions: Thinks Am is major
Confuses vi with V
Doesn't know chord roots

items.q: Write the basic home–away–tension–home progression in Roman numerals and in the key of G.
accept: I IV V I; G C D G
items.why: In G, degrees 1, 4 and 5 are G, C and D.

items.q: Your progression ends on V and sounds unfinished. What should you add, and why?
items.answer: Add I. V is the dominant, and its tension pulls back to the tonic.
accept: End on the tonic chord because V resolves to I
items.why: V creates tension that resolves to I.
